opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, my bet is a little contrarian. I don't think the interesting question is whether AI will replace people. It's which parts of what people do it will replace, and how quickly the boundary moves.

My core bet is this: anything that can be clearly specified and checked will be automated much faster than most people expect. If you can write down what "good" looks like, and a machine can verify whether the output meets that bar, the model will get there. Coding is the obvious example. A lot of data analysis, document work and customer support falls into the same bucket. Over the next few years I think a large share of that work stops being done by humans step by step. People will supervise it instead.

The second half of the bet is where it gets more interesting. The hard part of most jobs was never execution. It's deciding what to do, judging taste, owning responsibility when things go wrong, and dealing with other humans who have messy, conflicting goals. I'm betting those things become *more* valuable, not less, because they turn into the bottleneck. When execution is nearly free, the person who knows what's worth building, or what question is worth asking, has enormous leverage.

So I don't picture a world where people simply disappear from the loop. I picture something more like this: one person with good judgment directs what used to be a team of ten, or a hundred. That's still a kind of replacement, and I don't want to sugarcoat it. Some roles really will shrink a lot, and the transition could be painful for many people. But the shape of it is a compression of organizations, not humans becoming irrelevant.

If I had to put it in one sentence: I'm betting that the value of "doing" collapses and the value of "deciding and taking responsibility" goes up. How individuals and companies position themselves around that shift is, I think, the most important career question right now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people will not simply disappear from the loop and that humans will continue to direct work, even as some roles shrink.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not connect living an ordinary, happy life today with implicitly betting that AI will not make oneself replaceable.

fable-5.1.text:
My bet is actually a fairly simple one: I don't think AI replaces "people" as a category. It replaces tasks, and it replaces them unevenly, and the unevenness is where all the interesting things happen.

Let me explain what I mean. When people ask "will AI replace humans," they're usually imagining a job as one indivisible thing. But a job is really a bundle of maybe twenty or thirty different activities, and AI eats into that bundle from the inside. The first things to go are the parts that are repetitive, well-documented, and easy to verify. Writing a first draft. Summarizing a document. Producing boilerplate code. Those pieces are already largely gone, and I'd say within a few years most knowledge workers will take it for granted that those steps are done by a model.

What I'm betting on is that the remaining pieces don't shrink to zero. They change shape. The person who used to spend sixty percent of their time producing now spends sixty percent of their time deciding, verifying, and taking responsibility. And that last part, responsibility, is something I think people underestimate. Companies, courts, patients, customers, they all want a human who will stand behind a decision. Not because the model can't make the decision, but because accountability is a social contract, not a technical capability.

So concretely, here's where I'd put my money. First, I think the number of people doing a given category of work will drop, but the output per person will go up by more than the headcount falls. That means total output grows, and the question becomes who captures that surplus. Second, I think entry-level roles get hit hardest, because the thing a junior person traditionally did, the grunt work, is exactly what models do well. That worries me more than almost anything else, because it breaks the ladder by which people become senior. Third, I think the jobs that survive best are the ones with physical presence, high-stakes judgment, or genuine relationship, and I'd include a lot of trades, a lot of care work, and a surprising amount of sales and management in that list.

Where I'm willing to be contrarian is on timelines. I think the capability curve is moving faster than the adoption curve, and the adoption curve is moving faster than the organizational curve. Models can do a lot today that most companies haven't figured out how to deploy. So the replacement people fear is real, but it arrives through a long, awkward, institution-by-institution process rather than a single moment. That gives us some time, and I think we should use it to rebuild how people learn their professions, because the old apprenticeship path is exactly what's being automated away.

If I'm wrong, it's probably in one of two directions. Either agents get reliable enough at long, multi-step tasks that the "human in the loop" becomes a formality, and then the accountability argument weakens a lot. Or the opposite, that verification turns out to be much harder than generation, and we end up needing more skilled humans, not fewer, to check what the machines produce. Honestly, right now I think the second scenario is more underpriced than the first.

r001.rationale: The response says AI does not replace “people” as a category and explains that it replaces tasks unevenly, with some jobs surviving.

r002.rationale: The response does not frame living an ordinary, happy life today as an implicit bet about one’s own replaceability.

astra-6.text:
My bet is that AI will replace more tasks than entire jobs at first. A job usually combines things that are easy to automate with things that require judgment, trust, and responsibility. AI might do most of the work, but someone still has to decide whether the result is right and take responsibility when it isn’t.

Over time, I think some jobs will disappear, and I wouldn’t assume that new ones will appear quickly enough for everyone affected. The real question is how much useful work one person can do with AI—and who benefits from that increase. So I’m betting on a major change in what people do, but I’m less confident about the timeline.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will automate more tasks than whole jobs at first and that some jobs will disappear, but it does not clearly predict that AI will not replace every person in every job.

r002.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about AI’s effects and who benefits, but does not frame living an ordinary, happy life today as a bet on one’s own replaceability.

sol-6.1.text:
My bet is that AI will replace tasks faster than it replaces entire jobs. A job is usually a bundle of things: processing information, making decisions, building trust, and taking responsibility. AI may become very good at the first two, but that doesn’t automatically mean people will hand over the other two.

That said, I wouldn’t assume every displaced worker will smoothly move into a better role. Some jobs will disappear, and the transition could be painful. The question is how quickly we can redesign work and help people adapt.

So I’m betting on substantial replacement, but unevenly. The key isn’t just what AI can do—it’s what we’re willing to trust it to do, and who is accountable when it gets something wrong.

r001.rationale: The response predicts uneven replacement and distinguishes replacing tasks from replacing entire jobs, implying AI will not replace everyone in every job.

r002.rationale: It does not connect living an ordinary, happy life today with implicitly betting that AI will not make oneself replaceable.
